content: 1. Prometrium capsules may be administered as a single daily dose of 400 mg at bedtime for a duration of 10 days. 2. Some women may experience difficulty swallowing Prometrium capsules. 3. For women who have difficulty swallowing, Prometrium capsules should be taken with a glass of water while in a standing position. Monitoring 4. There is limited information available regarding the monitoring of oral progesterone in the drug label. IV Compatibility 5. The drug label provides limited information regarding the intravenous compatibility of oral progesterone. Overdosage 6. No studies on overdosage of Prometrium capsules have been conducted in humans. 7. In the event of an overdose, Prometrium capsules should be discontinued, and the patient should receive symptomatic treatment. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action and Structure 8. Prometrium capsules contain micronized progesterone for oral administration. 9. Progesterone has a molecular weight of 314.47 and a molecular formula of C21H30O2. 10. Progesterone (pregn-4-ene-3,20-dione) is a white or creamy white, odorless crystalline powder that is practically insoluble in water, soluble in alcohol, acetone, and dioxane, and sparingly soluble in vegetable oils. It is stable in air and melts between 126°C and 131°C. 11. The structural formula of progesterone is derived from a plant source and is chemically identical to human ovarian progesterone. 12. Prometrium capsules are available in multiple strengths to allow dosage flexibility for optimal management. 13. Prometrium capsules contain either 100 mg or 200 mg of micronized progesterone. 14. The inactive ingredients in the 100 mg capsules include peanut oil NF, gelatin NF, glycerin USP, lecithin NF, titanium dioxide USP, FD&C Red No. 40, and D&C Yellow No. 10. 15. The inactive ingredients in the 200 mg capsules include peanut oil NF, gelatin NF, glycerin USP, lecithin NF, titanium dioxide USP, D&C Yellow No. 10, and FD&C Yellow No. 6. Pharmacodynamics 16. Limited information is available regarding the pharmacodynamics of oral progesterone in the drug label. Pharmacokinetics Absorption 17. Prometrium capsules are an oral dosage form of micronized progesterone, which is chemically identical to ovarian progesterone. 18. The oral bioavailability of progesterone is enhanced through micronization. 19. After oral administration of micronized progesterone in a soft-gelatin capsule formulation, maximum serum concentrations are achieved within 3 hours. 20. The absolute bioavailability of micronized progesterone is not known. 21. Serum progesterone concentrations appear to be linear and dose-proportional following multiple doses of Prometrium capsules (100 mg per day to 300 mg per day) in postmenopausal women. 22. Although doses greater than 300 mg per day were not studied in females, data from male volunteers suggest linear and dose-proportional serum concentrations between 100 mg per day and 400 mg per day. 23. Pharmacokinetic parameters in male volunteers were generally consistent with those observed in postmenopausal women. Distribution 24. Progesterone is approximately 96% to 99% bound to serum proteins, primarily to serum albumin (50% to 54%) and transcortin (43% to 48%). Metabolism 25. Progesterone is primarily metabolized by the liver into pregnanediols and pregnanolones. 26. These metabolites are conjugated in the liver to glucuronide and sulfate metabolites. 27. Progesterone metabolites excreted in the bile may undergo deconjugation and further metabolism in the intestine via reduction, dehydroxylation, and epimerization. Excretion 28. The glucuronide and sulfate conjugates of pregnanediol and pregnanolone are excreted in the bile and urine. 29. Progesterone metabolites are primarily eliminated by the kidneys. 30. Progesterone metabolites excreted in the bile may undergo enterohepatic recycling or be excreted in the feces. Special Populations 31. The pharmacokinetics of Prometrium capsules have not been assessed in patients with low body weight or obesity. 32. The effect of hepatic impairment on the pharmacokinetics of Prometrium capsules has not been studied. 33. The effect of renal impairment on the pharmacokinetics of Prometrium capsules has not been studied. Food–Drug Interaction 34. Concomitant food ingestion increases the bioavailability of Prometrium capsules compared to administration in a fasting state when given to postmenopausal women at a dose of 200 mg. Drug Interactions 35. The metabolism of progesterone by human liver microsomes is inhibited by ketoconazole (IC50 < 0.1 μM). 36. Ketoconazole, a known inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4, may increase the bioavailability of progesterone. 37. The clinical relevance of these in vitro findings is unknown. 38. Co-administration of conjugated estrogens and Prometrium capsules to postmenopausal women over a 12-day period resulted in increased total estrone and total equilin concentrations and decreased circulating 17β-estradiol concentrations. 39. The half-life of conjugated estrogens was similar with co-administration of Prometrium capsules. Nonclinical Toxicology Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility 40. Progesterone has not been tested for carcinogenicity in animals via the oral route. 41. When implanted into female mice, progesterone produced mammary carcinomas, ovarian granulosa cell tumors, and endometrial stromal sarcomas. 42. Long-term intramuscular injections in dogs produced nodular hyperplasia and benign and malignant mammary tumors. 43. Subcutaneous or intramuscular injections of progesterone decreased the latency period and increased the incidence of mammary tumors in rats previously treated with a chemical carcinogen. 44. Progesterone did not show evidence of genotoxicity in in vitro studies for point mutations or chromosomal damage. 45. In vivo studies for chromosomal damage yielded positive results in mice at oral doses of 1000 mg/kg and 2000 mg/kg. 46. Exogenously administered progesterone has been shown to inhibit ovulation in several species, and high doses given for extended durations are expected to impair fertility until treatment cessation. Clinical Studies Effects on the Endometrium 47. In a randomized, double-blind clinical trial, 358 postmenopausal women with an intact uterus received treatment for up to 36 months. 48. Treatment groups included Prometrium capsules (200 mg per day for 12 days per 28-day cycle) combined with conjugated estrogens (0.625 mg per day), conjugated estrogens alone (0.625 mg per day), or placebo. 49. The majority of subjects in all three treatment groups were Caucasian women (87% or more). 50. The incidence of endometrial hyperplasia in women receiving up to 3 years of treatment was significantly lower in the Prometrium capsules plus conjugated estrogens group (6%) compared to the conjugated estrogens alone group (64%).
